prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological invariant of time-reversal-invariant insulators, and the experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part for B039, to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, with the citation scoped to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant. The round-1 exchange sharpened rather than weakened the case. Five members, from different fields, converge on it, but I rest it on the science. Kane and Mele showed that spin-orbit coupling in a time-reversal-invariant band insulator can produce a Z2-classified state with protected helical edge channels, and Molenkamp's group then grew HgTe quantum wells with the interface control and layer precision needed to see the predicted edge conduction. The chain from concept to measurement is short, the measurement was decisive, and the result has been confirmed for almost two decades in several materials and with several probes. In answer to the chair's question on what is new relative to 2016, a sentence the committee can defend is: the 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions and Hall-type phases whose protection needs broken time-reversal symmetry or specific model Hamiltonians, whereas this achievement is a topological classification of time-reversal-invariant band insulators realised in a real heterostructure. I also keep my materials-physics reason for caring about the Molenkamp part: without atomically controlled quantum wells there would have been no observation, and that is not a decoration on a theory prize. I have kept B022 and B001 as alternatives and left B003 out, because neither the discussion nor the chair's own statement has produced a defensible credit for it.
statement.case_against: The credit is incomplete and I do not think the citation can hide that. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal told Molenkamp's group which structure to grow and what to measure, Zhang is deceased, and the 3D topological-insulator work of Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others lies outside the trio; the three-laureate limit means no wording repairs this, and I rely on recollection for the priority history, which I have not checked. A second weakness is that the case is conceptual and materials-based, with limited applications so far. A third is that the optical lattice clock (B022) has a cleaner two-name allocation; if the committee concludes that an omission of this size makes a prize unfair, B022 is the configuration I would turn to, not a larger or looser topological prize. I would not accept the 2016 overlap as a reason to defer, but I accept that reasonable members weigh it differently.

responses.point: Kroll keeps B022 first because Katori and Ye give a clean allocation with no forced omission, argues that the pending redefinition of the second is irrelevant to physics merit, and ranks B039 eighth, while conceding that topological insulators have wider influence across condensed matter.
responses.response: I accept the redefinition argument and no longer treat it as a maturity requirement; independent clocks agreeing at the 10^-18 level are the evidence, and I withdraw the question I put to you in round 1 on timing. My disagreement is now narrower. Your own concession on breadth is the point: a tidy credit list is a reason to prefer a candidate when the science is comparable, but here the omitted-theorist problem is a cost of describing a real chain of events, and the same kind of gap exists for B022, where other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups stand outside the pair. I would ask whether you would support B039 if the citation names only the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect, since that is where all three names are decisive. For me the lattice clock remains a strong alternative, with the 2005 and 2012 lineage as the residual doubt.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes B022 with B003 (Halzen alone), a two-part prize of three laureates, but his own case_against calls the single-name credit for a collaboration-scale discovery the weakest part and says he would rather B022 or B039 stood alone if the attribution is judged too thin.
responses.response: I take you at your word on that last sentence. I think the committee has now judged the attribution too thin: no member other than you and the chair keeps B003 in a configuration, and the chair has moved it to an alternative. The diffuse flux is secure and I do not doubt it, but the statute asks us to name the people responsible for the original work, and one name for IceCube, with AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal outside it, does not do that. Pairing it with the clock would also give the lattice clock a partner chosen for breadth and not for a shared achievement. If you would stand B022 or B039 alone, I would ask you to say which, since that is the real choice left on the table.

responses.point: Eriksson supports B039 with a citation centred on the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification, treats 2016 as distinct, and asks the committee not to widen the credit to 3D materials, and he lists B035 (magic-angle graphene) as an alternative.
responses.response: We agree on the boundary and on the wording, and your round-1 point that the citation should state the HgTe realisation is one I have taken into the text. I would add one thing to your framing of the 2016 distinction: the clearest way to state it is that the earlier prize concerned phases whose protection depends on broken time-reversal symmetry or on a model system, and this one concerns a time-reversal-invariant band insulator found in a real, grown heterostructure. On B035 I side with Mehlig and Johansson: the origin of the correlated states is still debated and the experiments are about eight years old, so I do not put it beside B039.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B022 first and B039 second, separates the lattice clock from the comb because it solves the problem of interrogating many neutral atoms without perturbing the transition, and says B039 is the harder prize to write, not the weaker science.
responses.response: That last formulation is one I agree with, and it is close to my own view of the two: both are mature and well confirmed, and what separates them for me is how far the idea reaches and how clearly the citation can be drafted. Your account of why the clock is distinct from the comb has removed some of my doubt, and I have kept B022 as my first alternative for that reason. Where I still differ is on ranking. The clock is a major improvement in a measurement; band topology changed how electronic phases are classified, and that wider reach is why I place B039 first even with the visible omission. I also accept your point that the citation, not the head count, has to carry the attribution problem.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved B039 to the front after the opening ballots, scopes the citation to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 invariant, and says the omitted Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D work cannot be fixed by adding a name.
responses.response: I agree on the scope, and on the chair's question about how to avoid dismissing the omitted theorists, I think the answer is in what the citation claims. It should claim only what the three named people did: the Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall proposal, and the observation in HgTe. It should not say 'topological insulators' in general, because that would imply the 3D work and the HgTe prediction are credited to them, and a short sentence in the committee's accompanying explanation can acknowledge the prediction and the 3D developments as part of the field's history. I do not claim this fully answers the objection, since Zhang's absence is permanent, but it makes the omission a stated limit instead of a hidden one. I also agree with you that B003 should not be in a preferred configuration this year.

uncertainties: Whether a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant, with the HgTe prediction and 3D work acknowledged in the accompanying explanation, is enough to keep the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from reading as dismissal; I think it is, but I cannot show it.

My recollection of the priority history among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and the 3D theorists is unchecked; I regard the order of the 2005 proposal, the 2006 HgTe prediction and the 2007 observation as settled and the relative weight of the 3D contributions as open.
Whether the committee will accept the two-sentence distinction from the 2016 prize as sufficient, or whether some members will still see a third topology prize.
Whether B039 or B022 would be preferred by members who weigh a clean credit list more heavily than breadth; the choice between them is close for several members.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no documented tie to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye, Capasso, Faist or Cho. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague on the committee, not a candidate; his declared interest in superconducting circuits concerns B023, which is not in my configuration or alternatives. My interest in epitaxial interfaces and electron microscopy is field proximity to the HgTe quantum-well work, not a personal connection.
